verses.t: Mencius said, "How unbenevolent King Hui of Liang was! The benevolent extend from those they love to those they do not love; the unbenevolent extend from those they do not love to those they love." Gongsun Chou said, "What do you mean?" "King Hui of Liang, for the sake of territory, sent his people to war and had them torn to pieces. He suffered a great defeat, and when he was about to fight again, fearing he could not win, he drove the young men he loved, [even his own son,] to die for it. This is what I call extending from those he did not love to those he loved."

Mencius said, "In the Spring and Autumn Annals there are no righteous wars. That one was better than another, that there certainly was. A punitive expedition is one in which a superior attacks an inferior; states of equal rank do not launch punitive expeditions against one another."

Mencius said, "It would be better to have no Book of Documents than to believe everything in it. Of the 'Completion of the War' chapter, I accept only two or three strips. The benevolent man has no enemy in the world. When the most benevolent attacked the most unbenevolent, how could the blood have flowed so deep that it floated the pestles?"

Mencius said, "There are people who say, 'I am skilled at drawing up battle lines; I am skilled at waging war.' This is a great crime. If the ruler of a state loves benevolence, he will have no enemy in the world. When [Tang] marched south, the northern tribes complained; when he marched east, the western tribes complained, saying, 'Why does he leave us till last?' When King Wu attacked Yin, he had three hundred war chariots and three thousand elite warriors. The king said, 'Do not be afraid. I come to bring you peace, not to make enemies of the people.' And the people bowed their heads to the ground, like a mountain crumbling. To mount a punitive expedition, zheng, means to set right, zheng. When each wishes to be set right himself, what need is there for war?"
Mencius said, "A carpenter or a wheelwright can give a person the compass and square, but he cannot make him skillful."

Mencius said, "When Shun was eating dried rice and wild greens, it was as if he would do so all his life. When he became Son of Heaven, wearing embroidered robes, playing the zither, and attended by the two daughters [of Yao], it was as if he had always had these things."

Mencius said, "Only now do I know how grave a thing it is to kill a man's kin. If you kill a man's father, he will kill your father; if you kill a man's elder brother, he will kill your elder brother. So although you do not kill them yourself, you are only one step removed."
Mencius said, "In ancient times border passes were set up to guard against violence. Today border passes are set up to commit violence."

Mencius said, "If you do not walk in the Way yourself, it will not be followed even by your wife and children. If you do not employ others according to the Way, you will not be able to employ even your wife and children."
Mencius said, "One who is well provided with profit cannot be killed by a year of famine. One who is well provided with virtue cannot be led astray by a corrupt age."
Mencius said, "A man who loves fame may be able to give up a state of a thousand chariots; but if he is not the right kind of man, a basket of rice or a bowl of soup will show in his face."

Mencius said, "If the benevolent and worthy are not trusted, the state will be empty. Without ritual and righteousness, superiors and inferiors fall into disorder. Without proper government, there will not be enough wealth to meet expenses."
Mencius said, "There have been people who gained a state without being benevolent, but there has never been anyone who gained the whole world without being benevolent."

Mencius said, "The people are the most important, the altars of the soil and grain come next, and the ruler is the least important. Therefore whoever wins the hearts of the common people becomes Son of Heaven; whoever wins the favor of the Son of Heaven becomes a feudal lord; whoever wins the favor of a feudal lord becomes a great officer. If a feudal lord endangers the altars of the soil and grain, he is replaced. If the sacrificial animals are perfect, the grain in the vessels is pure, and the sacrifices are offered at the proper times, and still there is drought or flood, then the altars of the soil and grain are replaced."

Mencius said, "A sage is a teacher for a hundred generations: such were Bo Yi and Liuxia Hui. So when people hear of the character of Bo Yi, the grasping man becomes clean-handed and the weak man gains a resolute will; when they hear of the character of Liuxia Hui, the shallow man becomes sincere and the mean man becomes generous. They rose up a hundred generations ago, and a hundred generations later there is no one who hears of them who is not stirred. Could they have done this if they were not sages? How much more did they stir those who were close to them in person!"
Mencius said, "Benevolence is what it is to be human. Put the two together and you have the Way."

Mencius said, "When Confucius left Lu, he said, 'Slowly, slowly I go.' This is the way to leave the state of one's father and mother. When he left Qi, he took up his rinsed rice and set off at once. This is the way to leave another state."
Mencius said, "That the gentleman [Confucius] was in distress between Chen and Cai was because he had no connections with the rulers above or the officials below."

Mo Ji said, "I am greatly slandered by people's tongues." Mencius said, "There is no harm in that. A scholar is especially hated by the many tongues. The Ode says, 'My grieving heart is deeply troubled; I am hated by the crowd of petty men.' That applied to Confucius. 'Though he could not quell their anger, he did not lose his good name.' That applied to King Wen."
Mencius said, "The worthy used their own clear understanding to make others understand clearly. Today people try to make others understand clearly while they themselves are in the dark."
Mencius said to Gaozi, "A footpath on a mountainside, if used constantly for a while, becomes a road. If it goes unused for a while, it is choked with grass. Now your heart is choked with grass."

Gaozi said, "The music of Yu was superior to the music of King Wen." Mencius said, "Why do you say that?" "Because the knobs of his bells are worn nearly through." "How does that prove it? Are the ruts at the city gate made by the strength of a single pair of horses?"

There was a famine in Qi. Chen Zhen said, "The people of the state all think that you, Master, will again have the granary at Tang opened for them. I suppose you cannot do it again." Mencius said, "To do so would be to act like Feng Fu. There was a man of Jin named Feng Fu who was good at seizing tigers with his bare hands, but in the end he became a respectable scholar. Once he went out into the countryside, where a crowd was chasing a tiger. The tiger had its back to a corner of the hills, and no one dared approach it. When they saw Feng Fu in the distance, they ran to meet him. Feng Fu rolled up his sleeves and got down from his carriage. The crowd were all delighted, but those who were scholars laughed at him."

Mencius said, "The way the mouth relates to flavors, the eye to colors, the ear to sounds, the nose to smells, and the four limbs to ease and rest: these are nature, but there is destiny in them, and so the gentleman does not call them nature. The way benevolence relates to father and son, righteousness to ruler and minister, ritual to guest and host, wisdom to the worthy, and the sage to the Way of Heaven: these are destiny, but there is nature in them, and so the gentleman does not call them destiny."

Haosheng Buhai asked, "What kind of man is Yuezheng Zi?" Mencius said, "A good man, a trustworthy man." "What do you mean by good, and what do you mean by trustworthy?" "What is desirable is called good. To have it in oneself is called trustworthy. To have it in full measure is called beautiful. To have it in full measure and shining forth is called great. To be great and transforming others is called sage. To be sage and beyond understanding is called divine. Yuezheng Zi is between the first two and below the last four."

Mencius said, "Those who flee from the Mohists are sure to turn to the followers of Yang; those who flee from the followers of Yang are sure to turn to the Confucians. When they turn to us, we should simply accept them. Those who argue with the followers of Yang and Mo today are like people chasing a stray pig: once it is back in its pen, they go on to tie up its legs."

Mencius said, "There are levies of cloth and thread, levies of grain, and levies of labor. A gentleman imposes one and defers the other two. If he imposes two at once, people will starve; if he imposes all three at once, fathers and sons will be separated."
Mencius said, "A feudal lord has three treasures: his land, his people, and his government. One who treasures pearls and jade will surely bring calamity upon himself."

Pencheng Kuo took office in Qi. Mencius said, "Pencheng Kuo is a dead man!" Pencheng Kuo was in fact killed. Mencius's disciples asked, "How did you know, Master, that he would be killed?" "He was a man of some small talent who had never learned the great Way of the gentleman. That was just enough to get himself killed."

Mencius went to Teng and was lodged in the Upper Palace. A pair of sandals that was being made had been left on a window sill, and the keeper of the lodging looked for them but could not find them. Someone asked Mencius, "Is this how your followers hide things away?" Mencius said, "Do you think they came here to steal sandals?" "Probably not. But you, Master, have set up your teaching so that you do not pursue those who leave and do not turn away those who come. If they come with a mind to learn, you simply accept them."

Mencius said, "All people have things they cannot bear to do; to extend this to what they can bear to do is benevolence. All people have things they will not do; to extend this to what they will do is righteousness. If people can fill out the heart that does not wish to harm others, their benevolence will be more than they can use. If people can fill out the heart that will not break through walls or climb over them [to steal], their righteousness will be more than they can use. If people can fill out the reality of refusing to be addressed with contempt, they will act righteously wherever they go. When a scholar speaks when he should not speak, he is using speech to fish for something; when he does not speak when he should speak, he is using silence to fish for something. Both are of the same kind as breaking through walls and climbing over them."

Mencius said, "Words that are simple but far-reaching in meaning are good words. A way of holding to what is essential that has wide effects is a good way. The words of the gentleman do not go beyond what lies before his eyes, yet the Way is in them. What the gentleman holds to is cultivating himself, and the world is brought to peace. People's fault is that they neglect their own fields and weed other people's fields: what they demand of others is heavy, and what they take upon themselves is light."

Mencius said, "Yao and Shun had it by nature; Tang and Wu returned to it. When every movement and expression, every turn and gesture, accords with ritual, that is the height of abundant virtue. Weeping for the dead with true grief is not done for the sake of the living. Following virtue steadfastly without swerving is not done in order to seek office. Being always true to one's word is not done to show that one's conduct is upright. The gentleman acts according to the law [of right] and simply waits for what is destined."

Mencius said, "When speaking to men of great position, think little of them and do not look at their grand and lofty airs. Halls many ren high, with beams projecting several feet: if I had my wish, I would not have them. Food spread out ten feet square before me, and concubines by the hundreds: if I had my wish, I would not have them. Feasting and drinking for pleasure, galloping on the hunt with a thousand chariots following behind: if I had my wish, I would not have them. Everything they have is what I would not have; everything I have is in accordance with the institutions of antiquity. Why should I stand in awe of them?"

Mencius said, "For nourishing the heart nothing is better than having few desires. If a man has few desires, though there may be some things in him that are not preserved, they will be few. If a man has many desires, though there may be some things in him that are preserved, they will be few."

Zeng Xi was fond of jujubes, and [after his death] Zengzi could not bear to eat jujubes. Gongsun Chou asked, "Which is more delicious, minced and roasted meat or jujubes?" Mencius said, "Minced and roasted meat, of course!" Gongsun Chou said, "Then why did Zengzi eat minced and roasted meat but not jujubes?" "Minced and roasted meat is a taste everyone shares; jujubes were his father's particular taste. We avoid speaking a person's personal name but not his surname, because the surname is shared while the personal name is his alone."

Wan Zhang asked, "When Confucius was in Chen he said, 'Why not go home? The young men of my school are ambitious and hasty; they press forward but do not forget their early ways.' When Confucius was in Chen, why did he think of the ambitious scholars of Lu?" Mencius said, "Confucius said, 'If I cannot find people who walk the middle way to associate with, I must turn to the ambitious and the cautious. The ambitious press forward; the cautious have things they will not do.' Did Confucius not want people of the middle way? Since he could not be sure of finding them, he thought of the next best." "May I ask what kind of people could be called ambitious?" "People like Qin Zhang, Zeng Xi, and Mu Pi were the ones Confucius called ambitious." "Why were they called ambitious?" "Their aims were grand and boastful. They kept saying, 'The ancients! The ancients!' But when one examined their conduct, it did not match their words. When even the ambitious could not be found, he wanted to find scholars who disdained anything unclean, and to associate with them. These were the cautious, who come next again. Confucius said, 'The only ones who pass my gate without entering my house and whom I do not regret are the village worthies. The village worthy is the thief of virtue.'" "What kind of person can be called a village worthy?" "[The village worthy says of the ambitious,] 'Why are they so grand and boastful? Their words take no account of their deeds, and their deeds take no account of their words, yet they keep saying, "The ancients! The ancients!"' [And of the cautious,] 'Why do they walk alone so coldly aloof? Being born into this age, one should be of this age. To be thought good by it is enough.' One who fawns on the world with hidden motives is a village worthy." Wan Zhang said, "If the whole village calls him an honest man, and wherever he goes he acts as an honest man, why did Confucius regard him as the thief of virtue?" "If you try to criticize him, you can find nothing to point to; if you try to censure him, there is nothing to censure. He goes along with the prevailing customs and fits in with a corrupt age. In his dwelling he seems loyal and trustworthy; in his conduct he seems honest and pure. Everyone is pleased with him, and he thinks himself right. Yet one cannot enter with him into the Way of Yao and Shun. That is why he is called the thief of virtue. Confucius said, 'I hate what seems to be but is not. I hate darnel, for fear it will be confused with grain. I hate glibness, for fear it will be confused with righteousness. I hate a clever tongue, for fear it will be confused with good faith. I hate the music of Zheng, for fear it will be confused with true music. I hate purple, for fear it will be confused with vermilion. I hate the village worthy, for fear he will be confused with the virtuous.' The gentleman simply returns to the constant standard. When the constant standard is set right, the common people are roused [to goodness]; when the common people are roused, there will be no perversity or wickedness."

Mencius said, "From Yao and Shun to Tang was more than five hundred years. Men like Yu and Gao Yao saw them and knew [their Way]; Tang heard of it and knew it. From Tang to King Wen was more than five hundred years. Men like Yi Yin and Lai Zhu saw him and knew [his Way]; King Wen heard of it and knew it. From King Wen to Confucius was more than five hundred years. Men like Taigong Wang and San Yisheng saw him and knew [his Way]; Confucius heard of it and knew it. From Confucius to the present is a little over a hundred years. We are so little removed from the age of the sage, and so very near the place where the sage lived. Yet if there is no one [who saw and knew], then there will indeed be no one [who hears and knows]."
